title: Standard vs Certification vs Accreditation — The Single Biggest ISO Exam Trap
shortDescription: ISO writes the rulebook. It does not check your homework. Someone else does that — and someone else checks THEM.
genZNote: Vibes are not a quality-control method — and neither is assuming ISO personally certifies every factory on Earth.

sections.heading: The Core Misconception to Avoid
sections.body: A huge number of exam-takers (and honestly, a huge number of working professionals) believe 'ISO certifies companies'. IT DOES NOT. ISO's entire job stops at PUBLISHING a standard. Everything after that — checking whether an organization actually follows the standard, and issuing a certificate saying so — is done by separate, independent bodies. This single distinction is one of the most consistently tested ISO facts in competitive exams.

rows: ISO (and national bodies like BIS, which adopt/adapt ISO standards)
A published document defining requirements (e.g. ISO 9001)
Independent CERTIFICATION BODIES (private companies, e.g. Bureau Veritas, SGS, TUV, or national bodies' certification arms)
A certificate stating an organization conforms to a standard
National ACCREDITATION BODIES (e.g. NABCB in India, part of the Quality Council of India)
Formal recognition that a given certification body is itself competent to issue certificates
Legal requirement to hold a specific certification, in specific sectors only

sections.heading: Key Definitions
bullets: Standard — a documented set of requirements, specifications, or guidelines developed by consensus, intended for common and repeated use.
Technical Specification — similar to a standard but published without requiring the same full consensus level — often used for emerging areas where full consensus isn't yet possible.
Conformity — the fulfilment of a specified requirement (i.e., actually meeting the standard's criteria).
Certification (third-party conformity assessment) — an independent body's written assurance that a product, process, system, or person meets specified requirements.
Accreditation — formal, independent recognition that a certification/testing/inspection body is competent to carry out specific conformity-assessment tasks.
Audit — a systematic, independent examination to determine whether activities comply with planned arrangements (i.e., whether a management system standard is actually being followed in practice).
Management system — the set of interrelated policies, processes and procedures an organization uses to achieve its objectives (e.g. a Quality Management System under ISO 9001).

sections.heading: Types of ISO Standards
bullets: Management system standards — define requirements for HOW an organization runs a system (e.g. ISO 9001 for quality, ISO 14001 for environment).
Product standards — define technical requirements for a specific product (e.g. dimensions, safety features).
Process standards — define requirements for how a specific process should be carried out.
Terminology/vocabulary standards — standardize definitions and terms used across an industry (e.g. ISO 9000, which defines the vocabulary the ISO 9001 family uses).

sections.heading: Why This Distinction Is the Actual Exam Trap
bullets: 'ISO certified' is a common phrase, but strictly it should mean 'certified BY AN INDEPENDENT BODY as conforming to an ISO standard' — ISO itself issues no certificates.
A certification body's own legitimacy depends on ITS accreditation — an unaccredited certification body can still issue a certificate, but it carries far less credibility.

This is why 'NABL-accredited laboratory' (a lab accredited BY NABL) and 'ISO 17025 certified laboratory' are talking about two connected but distinct facts: which standard it follows, and who confirmed it follows that standard.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: ISO develops standards; independent certification bodies certify organizations against those standards; accreditation bodies certify that the certification bodies themselves are competent — three separate layers, not one.
keyFacts: ISO does NOT certify any company, product, or person, anywhere, ever.
Certification = done by independent certification bodies (private companies or national bodies' certification arms).
Accreditation = a check on the certification body's own competence, done by a national accreditation body.
In India: NABCB (under the Quality Council of India) is the national accreditation body; NABL is the specific accreditation body for testing/calibration/medical laboratories.
commonConfusion: 'ISO certified' is shorthand — ISO itself never certifies; an independent, ideally accredited, certification body does.
Certification (checking an organization) and accreditation (checking a certification body) are two different layers, not synonyms.

highYieldFacts: ISO writes standards. It does NOT certify companies — independent certification bodies do that.
Accreditation bodies check the competence of certification bodies — a layer ABOVE certification, not a substitute for it.
A management system standard (e.g. ISO 9001) defines HOW an organization runs a system; a product standard defines requirements for a specific product.
commonTraps: Never write or imply 'ISO certifies companies' — this is the single most commonly tested ISO misconception.
Do not use 'certification' and 'accreditation' interchangeably — accreditation is specifically about certifying the certifiers.
mustRemember: Four-layer chain: Standard (ISO) → Certification (certification body) → Accreditation (accreditation body) → Regulation (government, where applicable).
ISO standards are voluntary by default; they become mandatory only via specific law or contract.

confusedTerms.distinction: Certification is a body's assessment of an ORGANIZATION against a standard; accreditation is a higher-level assessment of whether that CERTIFICATION BODY itself is competent to do the certifying.

possibleQuestions: Does ISO itself certify companies as compliant with its standards?
What is the difference between a certification body and an accreditation body?
